clinicalPearls: A genetically heterogeneous group of autosomal recessive disorders of melanin biosynthesis affecting skin, hair, and eyes, with OCA1 (tyrosinase/TYR), OCA2 (OCA2/P gene), OCA3 (TYRP1), and OCA4 (SLC45A2) accounting for most cases.
OCA1A reflects complete tyrosinase deficiency with lifelong white hair, milky skin, and translucent blue-grey irides, whereas OCA1B (yellow variant) permits some pigment accumulation with age.
The ocular phenotype is the diagnostic core: congenital nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia, reduced visual acuity, iris transillumination, and photophobia occur across all subtypes.
Misrouting of the optic nerve fibres at the chiasm, with excessive decussation, is a defining neuro-ophthalmic feature demonstrable on visual evoked potentials.
Cutaneous melanin deficiency confers a markedly increased lifetime risk of actinic damage, squamous and basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma, mandating lifelong sun protection.

Syndromic albinism must be excluded: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (bleeding diathesis, pulmonary fibrosis, ceroid deposition) and Chediak-Higashi syndrome (immunodeficiency, giant granules) are life-limiting mimics.
TYR mutations remain heat-sensitive in the temperature-sensitive variant, producing darker hair at cooler acral sites analogous to the Siamese-cat pattern.
Skin and hair colour vary widely between and within subtypes and ethnic backgrounds, so ocular signs rather than degree of cutaneous pigment guide diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Oculocutaneous albinism results from mutations that reduce or abolish melanin synthesis within otherwise structurally normal melanocytes. In OCA1 the defect lies in tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme catalysing the conversion of tyrosine to dopaquinone; complete deficiency (OCA1A) yields no melanin, while partial activity (OCA1B) permits limited pigment. Other subtypes disrupt melanosomal proteins that regulate melanosome pH, maturation, and tyrosinase trafficking: the OCA2 (P) protein and SLC45A2 (MATP) influence melanosomal acidification and enzyme processing, and TYRP1 stabilises tyrosinase and directs eumelanin synthesis. The resulting hypomelanosis affects the developing eye, where melanin is required for normal foveal development and correct routing of retinal ganglion cell axons; its absence produces foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, and abnormal chiasmal decussation. In the skin, absent melanin removes the natural photoprotective shield, accelerating ultraviolet-induced mutagenesis and photoageing.
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive ophthalmological assessment including visual acuity, nystagmus evaluation, and fundoscopy for foveal hypoplasia
Visual evoked potentials demonstrating chiasmal misrouting
Molecular genetic panel testing (TYR, OCA2, TYRP1, SLC45A2 and syndromic genes)
Full blood count and platelet aggregation studies where Hermansky-Pudlak or Chediak-Higashi is suspected
Peripheral blood film for giant granules in neutrophils (Chediak-Higashi)
Regular dermatological surveillance with dermoscopy for cutaneous malignancy
redFlags: Easy bruising or bleeding suggesting Hermansky-Pudlak platelet dysfunction
Recurrent severe infections or a hyperinflammatory (accelerated) phase indicating Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Progressive respiratory decline from pulmonary fibrosis in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome
New, changing, or ulcerated cutaneous lesion suspicious for skin cancer
Neurological deterioration pointing to a syndromic or alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Isolated oculocutaneous albinism is compatible with a normal lifespan, though visual impairment is lifelong and non-progressive, and diligent photoprotection substantially reduces the otherwise high risk of skin malignancy. Syndromic forms such as Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi carry a markedly worse prognosis owing to bleeding, pulmonary, or immunological complications.
pitfalls: Assuming visible skin or hair pigment excludes albinism, when ocular features are the true diagnostic key
Missing syndromic albinism by failing to enquire about bleeding, infection, or pulmonary symptoms
Under-emphasising lifelong photoprotection and skin cancer surveillance in darker-skinned patients
Confusing OCA with X-linked ocular albinism, which spares the skin and affects mainly males
Neglecting low-vision aids and educational support, thereby compounding avoidable disability
references: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine, current edition
Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
management: No curative therapy; lifelong rigorous photoprotection with high-factor broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing and sun avoidance to reduce skin-cancer risk
Regular dermatological surveillance with dermoscopy for basal and squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma, with prompt excision of suspicious lesions
Optimisation of vision with refractive correction and tinted or photochromic lenses for photophobia, plus low-vision aids and rehabilitation
Orthoptic management of congenital nystagmus and strabismus, with squint or nystagmus surgery in selected cases
Exclusion of syndromic albinism such as Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes, which alter prognosis and management
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with testing of at-risk relatives
Multidisciplinary care with educational and occupational low-vision support
